articles.headline: White House report card: Trump jets across the world while the home front burns
keyFacts: President Donald Trump took a diplomatic trip to Asia, ending with a trilateral summit in China alongside Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
During Trump's trip, domestic challenges mounted, including major tech infrastructure outages, economic uncertainty, and reported threats against Cabinet members.
The China summit concluded with a four-point peace declaration, after which Trump returned to Washington for a scheduled briefing.
body: Welcome to Friday’s Washington Secrets . Is this the new normal? President Donald Trump went on a whirlwind trip to the Far East while his problems mounted at home. Plus, we look at the unlikely owner of some of Roy Cohn’s archives and rejoice at the prospect of Ron DeSantis launching a presidential bid, plant pots and all.

Like many a lame duck president, Donald Trump leaned into foreign affairs this week. He left behind devastating election results, a domestic electronic infrastructure crisis, uncertainty about JD Vance’s ability to take up the MAGA flame, stock market uncertainty, looming Democratic investigations, the withdrawal of the White House pick for Food and Drug Administration chief, in favor of hobnobbing with a dictator at war with Europe and a communist leader whose spies targeted the chief executive of one of America’s most important companies.

It started with Truth Social and a round of golf on Sunday. He broke his silence on the FAA ground stop that had halted flights across the country on Friday, blaming Joe Biden ‘s administration and saying “everything they touched turned bad.”

The president left for Asia on Monday morning, but managed to drop a bunch of headlines as he chatted to reporters on the South Lawn as he left the White House. He said he “may” meet North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un during his trip (spoiler alert: he didn’t) and played down the idea that Jensen Huang’s love interest was feeding intelligence to the Chinese.
Perhaps Nvidia would take back their chief executive, who resigned as details of the affair came to light?
“I would certainly not mind seeing that,” said Trump. “He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return.”
But not, it seems, the Nvidia board, which made clear they had accepted Huang’s resignation in unanimous fashion.

Trump landed in Manila the following afternoon. It was straight into a busy diplomatic day, which included the first Quad meeting (with Australia , India , and Japan ) of his second term, where he announced a maritime patrol aircraft exercise and an AI accelerator.

Then he signed what he called an “historic trade deal” with Thailand , but which was actually a Joint Statement on an “Agreement Between the United States of America and the Kingdom of Thailand on Reciprocal Trade,” not to be confused with the “Framework for a United States-Thailand Agreement on Reciprocal Trade,” which they signed last year. Is that clear?
Similar hyperbole followed an agreement with the Philippines the next day. Trump called it “the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made.” His hosts said nothing had been signed.

But the main event was still to come. Trump flew into China , where he was greeted at the steps of Air Force One by communist leader Xi Jinping , who never normally bothers coming to the airport, but showed willingness after the president welcomed him at Joint Base Andrews earlier this year.
Thursday was the final day of the whirlwind trip. And it brought the first-ever three-way summit between leaders of the U.S., China and Russia .

Before that, Trump sat for a Fox News interview, where he again defended Huang. He admitted he had brought up the issue with Xi and played down the idea that the former chief executive of a company central to a U.S. strategic interest was sleeping with a Chinese spy.
“Any pretty woman that comes from China, they considered her to be a spy,” Trump said.

The trilateral ended with a four-point “declaration toward peace” covering UN reform, refined petroleum supply, “respect for immunities” of state officials (which was a clear rebuke of the International Criminal Court ) and a reaffirmation that nuclear war cannot be won.
And then it was back to Washington, where he was due to spend the weekend at the White House after a press conference in the briefing room on Friday morning.
So what did our two political strategists make of it all?

You are reading Washington Secrets , a guide to power and politics in D.C. and beyond. It is written by Rob Crilly. You can reach him at secrets@washingtonexaminer.com with your comments, story tips, and suggestion s.
Jed Babbin: Grade C

While the Democrats concern themselves with impeaching the president and his Secretary of War — and the slew of investigations they’ll launch in January — there are a lot of other things going on in the world.

The president met with Xi and Vladimir Putin this week in China. They didn’t agree on much, but a memorandum was signed swearing off nuclear war between the three. There was little else of note from the Yalta-like conference amid the smiles of the participants.

Iranian threats to assassinate Trump’s Cabinet members have caused at least four cabinet members — Secretary of State Marco Rubio , Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent , Attorney General Todd Blanche and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth — to go into hiding at various military bases around the D.C. area. White House chief of staff Stephen Miller has apparently joined them.
Trump claimed, in his Veterans’ Day speech at Arlington Cemetery last week, that we have won the Iran war. If we’ve won, why are these people hiding?

Meanwhile, the “tech outages” seem to be multiplying, now including the supersecret National Security Agency , which specializes in code-breaking and listening in on foreign governments’ private conversations. The belief that the “outages” are computer hacks is growing, and foreign governments are certainly involved.
So who’s behind them? China? Russia? Iran? Any one of the three is probably to blame.
The NSA “outages” are particularly troubling. They seem to indicate a disruption of classified internal communications. That ain’t good for a whole bunch of reasons.
Our government wants us to believe there haven’t been computer hacks by other nations. Maybe there have been, and maybe there haven’t, but the longer this goes on, the more likely it is.

Meanwhile, the U.S. has apparently hinted at a land-for-peace deal in Ukraine, saying that if Ukraine traded the Donbas region to Russia, it might get into NATO. Previous land-for-peace deals haven’t worked — the deal Neville Chamberlain bragged about when he returned from a meeting with Hitler comes to mind.
John Zogby: Grade D-

Don’t you just hate it when coincidences coincide? This past week, there were major service outages at the world’s largest tech companies, banks, airlines, and hotel chains, as well as at the F.AA and the NSA’s internal communications system.
At first, it was explained as “outdated copper wiring.” Then, according to the script, most spokespersons said it was due to “transitioning” from analog to digital infrastructure.
I recall that over the years, when utility, cable, and banking companies make upgrades, they notify their customers of real or potential service disruptions.

Even more concerning, there was no one in charge at home. The president was too busy clinking glasses, eating fried chicken, and co-producing a big nothingburger in China. Plus, he gave a clear indication that he wasn’t troubled by life intervening at home.

His party lost the last two Senate seats being counted , wholesale inflation hit 6.5% annualized — the highest in almost 4 years — and the U.S. is no longer considered a country where measles has been eliminated. More Epstein files are due to be released by court order, and an investigation has been launched related to alleged slush funds from Arab leaders to the Trump family and friends.
Trump lost about $1 billion in crypto investments, and fellow investors may either be forced to eat that debt or take on new debt.

His choice to head the FDA was withdrawn because of her stance on vaccinations and for simply not being competent. Iran has widened its bombing of Bahrain and U.S. bases in other Arab countries. The stock markets tanked even as (or because) Anthropic held a record IPO. Gas prices have gone down.
But a very bad week and an even worse look.

Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance has not only found himself alone within the administration, but a new Emerson poll shows a huge slip in his race to be the 2028 GOP nominee. But gas prices are down!

John Zogby ( @ZogbyStrategies ) is the founder of the Zogby Survey and senior partner at John Zogby Strategies. His latest book is Beyond the Horse Race: How to Read Polls and Why We Should . His podcast with son, managing partner, and pollster Jeremy Zogby, can be heard here .
Exhuming McCarthy

There is much to enjoy in the new Roy Cohn biography by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark, American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump . Not least, the frequent acknowledgments that pop up throughout the photographs and in footnotes on facts and quotes: “The Roy Cohn Personal Archive, courtesy of Michael Stipe .”
Yes, that Michael Stipe. The lead singer of REM , one of the most influential American rock bands of the past half century.

It turns out that he is the owner of boxes and boxes of Cohn artifacts, which include his gold watch, a 50 milligram vial of Demerol, a silver cigarette box apparently given to him by Sen. Joe McCarthy (his boss when he worked on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations), as well as his unpublished memoir.
This is how the authors describe meeting Stipe after hearing that he owned a handful of Cohn photographs.

Stipe reminded us that back in 1987 R.E.M. had a hit song called “Exhuming McCarthy.” I had often jogged to it and his other music. Stipe had always been curious about Roy Cohn’s life story, and so years later, when he happened across a collection of Roy Cohn memorabilia being sold at a New York auction house, he made a successful bid for the material. It turned out to be a treasure trove of artifacts…
Quote of the day

There’s a great interview with Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) in the New York Times . If you saw him on the stump in 2024 (as Secrets did), then you may be surprised by the idea that he is clearly mulling another run for president.
And DeSantis demonstrates that he has not lost any of the skills that saw him crash out of the Republican primary after losing by 30 points to Trump in the Iowa caucuses.
Here he is explaining why he has no interest in joining the Supreme Court.

“To say that you’re going to end up a potted plant on the Supreme Court and just kind of sit there,” he said, “and I respect the justices, and people like Clarence Thomas have been heroes of mine for many years, but it just — it’s totally contrary to what I’ve demonstrated and brought to the table.”
Secrets , for one, encourages him to run.
Lunchtime reading
A child support fight exposed a Trump adviser’s $15 million income : Nice work if you can get it. This court case exposes just how much money aides can make from proximity to the president.

Xi Jinping’s say-nothing summi t : What is it like to be a reporter covering a major international summit? “My hotel had an APEC information desk in the lobby, but the friendly young people behind it were unable or unwilling to tell me where the APEC summit would be held.”

articles.headline: All My Time Meant For GTA 6 This Week Is Being Taken Away By A Volleyball Game
keyFacts: The newly released 3D volleyball video game Just Volleyball has unexpectedly consumed the author's gaming time intended for Grand Theft Auto 6.
Developed by Temkosoft, Just Volleyball features detailed mechanics for positioning, timing, and aim, earning an overwhelmingly positive score on Steam.
The author noted minor flaws in Just Volleyball, such as the lack of proper rotation rules and net fault detection, but praised its overall gameplay.
body: Any attempt I've made to keep playing real-life volleyball in my 30s has led to me injuring myself in some way, so turning to volleyball video games has been my go-to for continuing to enjoy my favorite sport whenever I need to wait for my overworked knee to rest.

No game has really gotten all that close to capturing the sensation of what it's like to play the sport, however. I was really hoping Grand Theft Auto 6 would satisfy that need somehow--beach volleyball is pretty big in any coastal place that's warm--but if there's a way to participate in a volleyball match in Rockstar's open world game the same way you can fish or play golf, I haven't found it.
Spikair Volleyball is still one of the best volleyball games all these years later.

It's not like I don't have other games I could turn to for volleyball, but they each carry their own issues. Volleyball is the weakest part of Sports Story by a significant margin, and that game is already pretty bad . And while volleyball is the best part of Switch Sports, not everyone in that game's community understands how blocking is supposed to work . In terms of mechanics, Spikair Volleyball has been my favorite option for a while , but I don't really want a 2D volleyball game in which I control my entire side of the court. I want a 3D action-oriented volleyball game that's like Rematch , one that encourages my friends and me to work together to pull off seemingly superhuman plays.
It really seemed like I'd go another year without a good volleyball game. But then, this November, a dark horse appeared.

Released just prior to GTA 6 (it would have come out sooner, but instead released against the juggernaut because of the Steam review backlog issues ), Just Volleyball has proven to be fantastic. I've been enjoying it so much that all of the time I had previously set aside this week to play GTA 6 is being taken up by Just Volleyball instead.
It's super satisfying to avoid a block with a perfectly aimed spike.

It's just what I wanted: a volleyball game that plays like Rematch. Each player has to consciously move their sole character to the ball in order to interact with it, taking into account speed and arc to determine where it's going to fall.

Just Volleyball isn't easy, either. The game kicked my ass at first as I struggled to learn how everything works. There are mechanics tied to bumping, diving, setting, jumping, blocking, spiking, and serving--it makes for a fairly jam-packed tutorial, and you're warned that there are plenty of other, more advanced strategies (jump serves, float serves, setter dumps, among others) that the tutorial doesn't cover and that you'll just have to learn to do yourself.
I wish the sand court actually affected your character's movement.

The game takes into account not only which move you choose to interact with the ball, but which direction you're facing, and what spot on the court you're trying to get the ball to, and the ball's overall momentum. The physics engine isn't as responsive as, say, Rematch, but it's pretty damn good, encouraging you to communicate with your teammates and be purposeful in getting into as ideal a position as possible before doing anything else.

It's like a shooter in that way, which is how volleyball should work. I love how Just Volleyball has a bunch of small details to really capitalize on positioning, timing, and aim--it takes into account where I'm looking when I'm spiking, lets me move my arms in midair while blocking to try and recover from a bad jump, and even lets my character's foot be a viable means of touching the ball if my hands happen to miss.
Switch Sports is the only volleyball game to come close to delivering as rewarding a sense of accomplishment when digging a spike.

So much of what games like Sports Story, Switch Sports, and Spikair Volleyball get wrong is that sports are as much about creative expression as they are about understanding the rules and being athletic. And that's really the best aspect of Just Volleyball, that the game allows you to express yourself not only in terms of what your character looks like, but how they behave. You can get better at the timing of receiving spikes and be your team's star receiver. You can practice a bunch of different tosses and approaches to be a pinch server. Or you can develop your own setting style that incorporates your character's hands and feet to keep every rally going.

And the developer, Temkosoft, seems to understand the community that has been clamoring for a game like this--almost every Steam Achievement is a direct reference to Haikyu, one of the most popular shonen sports manga/anime out there and the premiere pick for volleyball fans. This game is a celebration of what people love about volleyball, whether it's playing it in real-life or reading and watching stories involving it, and I just can't tear myself away from it.
The character creator is about as expansive as the one in Rematch.

Is Just Volleyball perfect? No. I wish the game took positions into account so that only the three players in the front row could jump at the net. It's weird to sometimes see four to six players all working in tandem to block at once--which is super illegal in volleyball. I also wish the game would register players touching the net, which should count as a fault.

These issues aside, however, I'm having a great time. The community for Just Volleyball is pretty small, but we all seem to be really loving the game if the Overwhelmingly Positive Steam score is any indication (the game is normally $8 but is discounted to $5 until November 24--go buy it and jump into the game!).

Maybe, if GTA 6 is hiding a stellar volleyball minigame, I'll give Rockstar's open-world sandbox another whirl. But for now, Just Volleyball is all I care about. Well, Just Volleyball and and a few other cool-looking new demos and game releases (that you should also be playing right now) .

articles.headline: Pochettino demands say on big United decisions; Arteta takes fantasy football action; Nations League draw – live
keyFacts: Mauricio Pochettino took charge as Manchester United manager and stated he expects to be involved in all major squad recruitment decisions.
Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola said that Pochettino will have a tactical advantage in their upcoming match because of his fresh appointment.
Manchester United decided not to take legal action against a drone operator who filmed Pochettino's first training session after the operator apologized and removed the footage.
body: It’s shaping up to be another day of bonkers scorelines at the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar. Belgium, to start with, edged past Vietnam by a wafer-thin margin, winning 3-2. Tajikistan beat Cuba 5-3, like you do. Spain popped five unanswered goals past China. It looks very much like Italy will be the day’s big winners, being as they are 6-0 up against Jamaica with just under 10 minutes to play. Also playing right now: Senegal v Croatia (currently 1-1), Cote d’Ivoire v Uzbekistan (1-0) and Fiji v Morocco (0-2). England failed to qualify, finishing bottom of their first-round group with zero points, behind Sweden, Scotland and Lithuania.

Here is the latest from Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca, who claims his players are not distracted by the “noise” around the club’s financial-rules case as he seeks to end their losing run. I wonder how many meetings inside the Etihad campus for Maresca and his advisors/bosses/lawyers to come up with the word “noise”.

City flew out of the blocks in the Premier League this season, winning their first seven games, but three straight defeats have left them six points behind leaders Arsenal. The 10-time English champions are still waiting to discover the extent of their punishment after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules.

I don’t think the players are thinking too much about that,” he said, “If we want to relate the noise with the defeats, Villa away, I think we had so many chances. Brighton here, the keeper was the man of the match. The Forest one [a 3-1 defeat], where Erling [Haaland] had the chance to [make it] 2-2. I don’t think the players are focused on the noise.
Manchester City host Fulham in the early kick-off on Saturday.
In adjacent news, I enjoyed this piece from yesterday.

I can’t quite put my finger on why but Mauricio Pochettino seems like a really good fit for Manchester United. Maybe he just looks good in the tracksuit. Here’s the latest from his pre-match press conference and it already sounds like the Argentinian is marking out his territory.
When you have working with the politics inside Tottenham, PSG, Chelsea and USMNT, you know you have to set your stall out early.

Hello everyone! We’ll start with a bit more from Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso, who has been speaking about the absence and importance of João Pedro. The Brazilian has not played since the 2-0 win over Everton on 17 October and will be unavailable again when Leeds visit Stamford Bride on Saturday. Pedro remains joint-second top scorer this season but Chelsea have scored only one Premier League goal from open play in the four games Pedro has missed.

“It’s not just the strikers that can score. We can score from set-pieces, from defenders, from midfielders. It’s teamwork. For sure João is an important player but we need to deal with this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying. We need to deal with it. It’s not that I’m going to look for one explanation. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player. If we do more things right, we could compete better and win at Sunderland, but there are a few things that had to be done. We want João Pedro back but I don’t want to make a big thing out of that.
Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner believes Liam Delap could score 20 goals a season if he improves his all-round game.

Forest’s £50m summer signing from Chelsea enjoyed his best day since joining the club with a double to sink Manchester City earlier this month and Glasner believes that game showcased how the 23-year-old can become even more of a threat.

“I think the City game was where he has his biggest strengths, when he has his pace and he can use his power. And, of course, he can finish with right and left,” said Glasner. “But we’re also working with him around his movements in the box where he has a lot of potential with his physicality.
“Sometimes we arrive in the right areas for assists and then he’s not in the right places. This is what he needs to improve.

“I always said he will have double figures regarding goals at the end of the season because this is just how he is. He should keep this and then work on the other parts of football, and then he maybe goes closer to 20 than 10.”
Daniel Farke wants to create another “bit of history” against Chelsea and end Leeds’ 27-year winless run at Stamford Bridge.

No wins and nine defeats in 11 visits to west London, mean Leeds haven’t won at Chelsea since 1999. On snapping that run, Farke said: “Of course for Leeds United, it’s always a bit [of a] special fixture to travel to London to play Chelsea. And we are very respectful, but definitely not fearful.
“We know we have to be at our very best in order to give us a chance to win some points. But this is also why we travel. We want to be competitive.
“Time to create a bit of history. There’s always a chance. I know it’s (been) a while, but it’s difficult.”

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso said at his Friday press conference that Joao Pedro, Maxence Lacroix and Reece James remain sidelined for Saturday’s Premier League clash with Leeds at Stamford Bridge, while Jorrel Hato and Jamie Gittens are also unavailable. However, Emiliano Martínez is available after his head injury and Moises Caicedo’s minutes were managed while on international duty with Ecuador so he should be fit to play.
Overlap, underlap or sit back? How Premier League teams use their full-backs

Overlapping. Underlapping. Inverted. Traditional. The role of full-back has evolved dramatically. Once a defensive-first position that provided some auxiliary attacking support, the role has developed into something far more multifaceted.

Just ask right-back Ben White, who – with Riccardo Calafiori on the left – has been an important figure in Arsenal’s superb start to the campaign. Talking a few years ago, he said: “Playing full-back the way [Mikel Arteta] wants is completely different to any other manager. To play full-back for him, you’ve got to be a centre-midfielder, a centre-back, a winger and a No 10.”

Between them, White and Calafiori have contributed to six goals for Arsenal already in the Premier League this season (White: three assists; Calafiori: one goal, two assists). No other defender has registered more than three goal involvements so far. The Arsenal duo are a great illustration of the impact full-backs can have. But, with the position more demanding than ever before, how does each Premier League team deploy theirs?

Enzo Maresca confirmed Matheus Nunes and Abdukodir Khusanov are both doubts for Manchester City’s clash with Fulham at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday. The City coach cut a relaxed figure when asked about the three successive league defeats his team suffered before the international break, believing his team are progressing nicely.
He said: “I was not thinking we were doing everything well when we won games, and I’m also not thinking we’re doing everything wrong when we’re losing games.

“We’ve played 16 official games and we’ve won 12, so 70 per cent. If you tell me this is [will happen] in the next 16 games, I will sign! My view is probably different from everyone else’s view. For me it’s just the beginning of something long. I’m very happy in the way we’re working while also being concerned about the things we need to do better.
“It’s a matter of balance that we need to improve. We review things. The idea is to continue in attack in the same way, creating chances, but finding a balance when we defend.” Dominic Booth
Pochettino will have element of surprise an Anfield, says Iraola
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola fears Mauricio Pochettino will have a tactical advantage over him on Sunday because the new Manchester United manager is coming in fresh.
Pochettino will be taking charge of United for the first time since leaving his role as USA national team coach to replace the sacked Michael Carrick.
With little to go on as to how Pochettino will setup his United side, Iraola is guessing.

“We’ve faced each other. Obviously he has a lot of Premier League games that we can look at, and we can look at games in the US, but they still have this small advantage,” said Iraola. “We don’t have references to prepare because they can go different ways that we don’t actually know.
“The staff have been working with them, so they are going to arrive well prepared. We don’t have the references that we have against other teams.”

One advantage Iraola could have looked to exploit was the drone footage posted on YouTube of Pochettino’s first training session at Carrington, but the Liverpool manager was quick to criticise the YouTube channel that posted the video.

“They were sending me the footage yesterday, but I think the important thing about this is that it shouldn’t be legal. It happened to Manchester United but it could happen to me in a training session in the future,” he said.
“It isn’t about the advantage, it is the fact that there is a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect.”
United not planning legal action against drone operator

Manchester United do not intend to take legal action against a drone operator who filmed Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session, but warned that anyone responsible for further incidents would face significant legal and financial risk.

The operator, who identifies himself as Colin but has not disclosed his full name, apologised earlier today for what he called a “total error of judgement” and removed the footage from his YouTube channel.

A club source told Reuters there was no security breach at the Carrington site and that, while it was unclear whether the incident breached drone laws, United believed it had breached a number of other laws.
The club source said the operator had done the right thing by apologising and removing the content without being contacted by United. Reuters
Pochettino finishes on a question about whether or not the timing is right for him to manage United by saying: “A club like Manchester United, you cannot turn down.”

Asked whether or not he missed the day-to-day club of club management, Pochettino replies: “Of course. We were missing [the pressure] a lot. We are animals of the grass. We like to feel the grass, we like to smell the grass and try to help the players improve everyday. It’s true that it’s a different job when you’re in the national teams, but at the same time you learn a lot and we are much better coaches now.”

Asked whether he thought was fit enough, Pochettino says: “When we arrive, I think we found a group of players that we propose to do the football that we feel. To be brave and be Manchester United. It is about proposing that idea to be brave and take it to the field.”
He adds that data, such as the running stats referenced in the question, needs to be taken in context and while it can tell a story it is not the whole story.
Hinting at the question that plagued Ruben Amorim about whether he is coach or manager: “I was in all my career a coach, head coach, manager. It does not change too much.”
However, Pochettino also makes it clear he expects to be a part of the recruitment process: “I know in the future I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that affect the squad.”
Pochettino confirms Bruno Fernandes will remain as captain: “Bruno is our captain and a very important player but other players have to feel they are important from the bottom to the top.
“We spoke yesterday, I spent three hours chatting with all the players individually yesterday. I think I missed some injured players but in the next few days we will talk with everyone.
“It was very nice contact. It is important to listen to the players and what they need to say about areas on and off the field.”
“I don’t think too much about the past,” adds Pochettino. “It is about building our own way here. Of course, we feel the support from the club and we start to work.
“The past is not going to help, to think about yesterday. We have been speaking to the players and the most important thing is to think about the next action.
“We feel the support and we are going to work really hard to help the players to perform. That is the priority.”

Pochettino says his target, after getting over the jet lag, is to get too know the people around the club and his players. He adds that his target is to “try and from the beginning have an impact. It is important to have a positive impact, that is our most important job.”

Pochettino is happy to be here, which is a good start. Asked how you create a culture, he says: “The players need to buy into the idea that we need to improve, that is our job. The job is to find a way from Sunday to perform and to start to get the results that that [United] historically need because Manchester United need to be in a different place than they are now.”

David Moyes has confirmed Jack Grealish is “fit and available” for Everton’s trip to Brentford on Monday, having missed the past four games through a combination of illness and for disciplinary reasons. Grealish played in a behind-closed-doors friendly against Derby last week and issued an apology for not being able to help the team. “He’s back in training and back in around the team,” said Moyes, who received a presentation from captain James Tarkowski and former player Leon Osman before his press conference on Friday. Moyes will manage Everton for the 593th time on Monday - breaking Harry Catterick’s club record.

Email from Dean Kinsella: “Well that Nation’s Cup draw couldn’t really have panned out much better for England. Norway (except for the big guy upfront) shouldn’t be too great an obstacle. While the two other main contenders, France and Spain battle it out. I’ll get the silver polish out.”

It’s like Dean has no experience of watching England at all. More broadly, as much as the Nations League is a significant improvement on international friendlies, do we count it as silverware? Would winning it be a bigger achievement than Le Tournoi?
Now news from Poland, where the national football federation says it has suspended 10 players competing in the lower divisions for suspected match-fixing.
The Polish Football Association (PZPN) said in a statement that the players were playing in the third division and lower, but did not indicate how long they will be suspended. Associated Press
Arsenal’s Lisa Baum: ‘I believe in us. I think it’s all about the small margins’

Lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

“It was unbelievable,” says Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”
Read Suzanne Wrack’s full interview with Lisa Baum:
Fabian Hürzeler: 'I've never had the feeling of leaving. I'm not done'

Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton coach, has given his press conference ahead of the game against Hull, and explained how, when and why he punishes players for not being sufficiently committed to their counter-pressing:

Counter-pressing is a law for us. Counter-pressing is not a decision you can do. It’s something you can do when you have a good day, when you have a bad day, when you’re in a bad mood, when you’re ready for a game or training, you can do it every day. It’s a non-negotiable for us. If you have the feeling the players are not on it then yeah, in some moments the players have to run. But we use it more in pre-season. As long as I’m happy with the counter-pressing we don’t need it.

Hürzeler says he’s not worried about drones taking footage of his training sessions. “No, because we have an airport next to us. So if they put a drone up I’m sure the drone won’t exist long, because it can cause some bad consequences. We don’t have this problem. We have other problems, with the aeroplanes, sometimes with the wind.

With the Brighton owner, Tony Bloom, having suggested this week that he could one day move to Bayern Munich, Hürzeler has committed his immediate future to the club, saying he “still has the feeling that I’m not done”:

To me it’s a privilege to work here. And of course in my time here there were a lot of rumours but I’m always fully committed to this club. I never had this feeling of leaving, because the club gives me a lot. I still go to bed and have the feeling that I’m not done. I still think there’s potential to get out of this team, to get out of this club.

articles.headline: Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
keyFacts: The Dutch Data Protection Authority advised consumers against buying AI smart glasses after safety tests revealed safety and privacy issues.
Regulators stated that tested glasses gave incorrect safety advice in simulations and permitted unauthorized nearby people to view recordings.
AP Vice Chair Monique Verdier urged Dutch and European politicians to consider these test results when developing future AI policy.
body: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.

The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.

In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call.
Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events.

The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role."

A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense.
"Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP.
"AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified."

The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary.
The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.
Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”
Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable.
The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.
"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them
However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders."
Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.
"It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said.
"Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience."
Smart specs can't shake the hate
When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.
"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons , and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces.
Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time.
Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.
On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones.
However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.
A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children.
There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy.
A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament.

The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

articles.headline: Mauricio Pochettino is right and Mark Cuban is wrong – US soccer is screaming for relegation change
keyFacts: Soccer figures including Thomas Muller and Mauricio Pochettino argued that Major League Soccer needs promotion and relegation to increase competitive pressure.
MLS commissioner Larry Berg and former sports owner Mark Cuban pushed back against adding relegation, citing financial stability, franchise fees, and investments.
Players like Tyler Adams expressed support for relegation to create more excitement and stakes for both fans and players.
body: Lionel Messi did not choose to sign with an MLS team because he wanted to play in the greatest football/soccer league in the world.

Messi chose to align himself with Inter Miami and David Beckham as he approaches 40 years old because the living Argentina legend wanted to keep playing the biggest sport in the world while building his global brand in America .
Messi leads MLS in scoring this season but is in the final era of his career AFP
Would MLS be better with relegation and promotion?
Of course, there are other reasons why the greatest footballer in history keeps scoring goals in Major League Soccer, which significantly trails the NHL in annual revenue.
Messi entered the weekend with 26 goals, ahead of the likes of Petar Musa and Sam Surridge.
That was during the same week when the pros and cons of relegation and promotion were debated from California and Florida to Manchester and London.
World Cup winner and Vancouver Whitecaps star Thomas Muller is the latest big name to call out the MLS topic that won’t go away.
“There is no relegation. There is no big pressure,” Muller told Global News. “There is, ‘Oh, yes, we do a rebuild.’
“Nobody is happy to lose, but it’s totally different when you fight for getting relegated.
“Maybe, you lose budget for the next year, the whole club. You lose people working at the club. When the budget changes, it’s totally different for fans.”
Muller won 33 trophies, including two Champions Leagues and 13 Bundesliga titles , so the Whitecaps midfielder knows what he speaks.

Vancouver also tops the MLS Western Conference with 64 points, which make Muller’s comments even more searing — especially after new Manchester United manager and former USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino effectively said the same thing .

“If you start in MLS and you haven’t won a game in three months and you’re at the bottom, what’s the consequence if there’s no promotion or relegation, no international competition?” Pochettino told El Pais.
Mauricio Pochettino wanted more out of soccer in the USA getty
Thomas Muller called out the ‘pressure’ of MLS football without relegation Getty
“American sports reward losers! But soccer is different: If you reward those who don’t win … If you don’t have goals, you don’t fight. If I lose, what happens? Nothing. They just fire the coach.”
Compare that passion to the words of new MLS commissioner Larry Berg, who immediately pushed back against adding real jeopardy to a soccer season.
“I can understand the appeal for the fans, (but) I don’t think it’s a great way to build a league,” Berg said in August.
“I don’t think it’s a way to get stadiums built, get training facilities built, and to have owners invest in rosters and all the other things you need to do.

“So the great thing about promotion and relegation for fans is that the jeopardy is quite severe. But I think there are other ways to create jeopardy during the regular season, (and) again in the play-offs, during the play-offs, to get to the next round. That’s what we want to focus on.”
What Berg could have said is that San Diego FC paid a whopping $500million expansion fee to enter MLS in 2023, and that is why Major League Soccer owners still fear relegation and promotion so much.
Tyler Adams spoke out in favor of MLS relegation to help the league getty
America’s best soccer players take their professional talent overseas Getty

The costs are too high, the real investment on return is still a long time away, and MLS is still trying to find a spot on the same TV that is dominated by the NFL, NBA , MLB , college football , college basketball, NHL, WNBA , auto racing, golf, tennis and so much more in America.
“ He (Pochettino) is wrong . If you need external motivation to compete, you shouldn’t be on the court/pitch/field, in any capacity,” former Dallas Mavericks owner Mark Cuban tweeted.
Ex-USMNT and Premier League goalkeeper Brad Friedel has seen both sides of the game in America and England.
Friedel’s words leading up to the historically large 2026 World Cup still stick with me five months later.
“No one’s making money in the football there, soccer there,” Friedel exclusively told talkSPORT.
“So my worry is, does this last for another ten years? Because, I mean, how many billionaires are out there, billionaire consortiums, that are going to pay $500million franchise fees?
Brad Friedel wondered about the financial future of MLS getty
Mark Cuban pushed back against Pochettino’s relegation rant Getty

“That’s why you see so many American owners coming over to Europe. Why? Because you own stadium, you own land, you own training ground. And you’re not paying $500 mil upfront for a franchise fee system that, if everyone keeps losing money, what happens with the franchise fee eventually?
“It invariably is going to go down — unless they get the media rights deal. If they get the media rights deal, then everything will be great.”
Pochettino and Muller are 100 per cent right — the lack of relegation and promotion are holding back soccer in America.

But when CF Montreal (MLS) is worth more than AFC Bournemouth (Premier League) and Burnley (Championship), it’s no wonder that MLS owners aren’t willing to watch their cash burn on the whims of one down year.
“I would like to see (promotion and relegation) in MLS, in the U.S. I think that would add to the competitive nature of the league,” USMNT and Bournemouth star Tyler Adams said in 2025.

“It just gives everyone a lot more to play for when you know there’s a risk of going down when you don’t play well, so it adds a little bit more pressure, adds a little bit more nerves and excitement for the fans as well. So hopefully one day it’s in MLS.”
MLS has made solid strides under Don Garber, who will step down as commissioner at the end of the year.
It’s on Berg and MLS owners to listen to the truth that Pochettino, Muller and others have spoken.
The power, pain and history of the English football pyramid can’t be recreated in the USA.
But there are other modern ways to make Major League Soccer more respected on a global stage.

body: Chinese police have arrested 13 individuals in Shanghai allegedly involved in a bootleg Final Fantasy 7 Tifa figurine business, after consumers reported the operation. They are currently being investigated on suspicion of selling infringing reproductions.
Reported by Gamespark, the police cracked down on the operation which involved the seizure of around $300,000 of goods related to the figurines.

The investigation started in May, after police received reports from concerned members of the public about the Tifa figurines. They were made from different materials than official figurines, and after confirming the illegitimacy of these products with the rights holders, Square Enix, police determined these businesses were not authorised to be producing such goods and went to work.

The appearance of these counterfeits were deemed identical to the real merch, and therefore the alleged crime was deemed infringement of official goods. These counterfeits also came in different sizes, some of which were more expensive than the originals and customisabile.

Looking at pictures taken by local outlet Shangguan News (and put side-by-side by Automaton), you can see the official Tifa figurine (right) next to the counterfeit version (left). Both show Tifa in a blue dress, though the materials used are clearly different.

articles.headline: Trump insists he's "not rushing to make any decisions on Iran"
keyFacts: President Trump said he is not rushing decisions on Iran, though sources said the U.S. and Israel consider near-term strikes.
Iran's foreign ministry rejected President Trump's allegations that the country may be developing chemical or biological weapons.
The U.S. Senate rejected a resolution that would have directed President Trump to remove American forces from hostilities with Iran.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:
- President Trump told an Israeli TV network on Thursday that he is "not rushing" and could wait until 2027 to make a decision on his next move in the .

- Despite Mr. Trump's remark, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News Israel and the U.S. are considering in the short term, with the Netanyahu administration concerned about how rapidly Iran is rebuilding its weapons production capacity.

- Iran on Thursday rejected Mr. that it may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, with the foreign ministry saying U.S. allegations "keep changing" and are following "the same fraudulent script" as the justification for the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq.
Saudi Arabia intercepts 2 Houthi missiles, coalition says
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Friday that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen's government in the impoverished nation's more than decade-long civil war against the Iran-backed rebel group.

The latest missiles launched by the Houthis targeted the Jazan region, on the southwest Saudi coast near the border with Yemen, but "air defense intercepted and destroyed" them, according to coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki.
The Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district earlier this week.
Cargo ship reports being fired on by assailants in small boat in Gulf of Aden
A bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, has reported shots being fired in its vicinity by armed men on a small boat, according to a British naval monitor.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center, which is run by the British navy, said Friday that the ship was traveling eastbound when it was approached "by a dark blue skiff with six unidentified, armed persons on board."

"Four shots were fired in quick succession from the skiff and warning shots were returned by the armed security team onboard the bulk carrier," UKTMO said, adding that there was no damage reported to the vessel or its crew.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis issue evacuation warning for Riyadh's financial district
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis urged people to avoid Riyadh's financial district Friday as the group issued a series of threats against Saudi Arabia.

"We announce that (King Abdullah Financial District) in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, is a military target for our forces. We therefore call on all employees, workers and citizens to stay away from it immediately," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.

In a Telegram post Friday, Saree wrote: "We renew our warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries. Saudi Arabia is not safe except for the holy areas in Mecca and Medina."
Saudi Arabia of damaging a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district with a strike earlier this week.
CBS/AFP
U.S. and Israel considering new assault on Iran, sources say
Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.

Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions.
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.

The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind.

For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.
Saudi's fight with Iran-backed Houthis intensifies as civilians warned to evacuate area around Yemeni port

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting in the escalating conflict with Iran's Houthi allies warned civilians Friday to leave the area around the key port of Hodeidah on Yemen's Red Sea coast, which has been held by the rebels for years.

The warning, issued in a social media post by the coalition's Saudi spokesman, suggested Saudi airstrikes on the port could be imminent. It came after Houthi authorities accused Saudi forces of killing 19 people earlier Friday with an attack that hit a civilian boat.

Yemen's civil war flared back up in July as the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran sent regional tension soaring. While the Yemen war started more than a decade ago with the Iran-backed Houthis seizing a huge portion of the country, including capital city Sanaa, it had been relatively calm for years until this summer.

Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi on Friday accused Saudi forces of a "horrific massacre" for the strike on the boat, which the rebels say killed civilians who had been displaced from their homes by the war.

Earlier Friday, the Saudi coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile and two drones fired at the kingdom's southern region, and the Saudi civil defense agency issued warnings of "potential danger" for the cities of Jizan and Abha, as well as the Khamis Mushait Governorate — all in the south.
They later said the danger had passed.
CBS/AFP
Trump's comments on chemical and biological weapons follow "same fraudulent script," Iranian official says

Iran's foreign ministry rejected on Thursday President Trump's accusation that the country may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, comparing the claims to then-Secretary of State Colin Powell asserting to the United Nations that Iraq had obtained weapons of mass destruction.

"After the grand narrative of the 'Iranian nuclear threat,' U.S. officials are now claiming that there are indications Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons!" Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X. "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar. Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."

Baqaei cited the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003, which Washington justified with the claim of weapons of mass destruction being developed by Saddam Hussein's government, and asked why Americans would fall for it again.

"Do American officials really expect the world to forget Colin Powell's infamous appearance before the U.N. Security Council in 2003, when he held up a small vial as a visual representation of the alleged threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction?" he asked. "That moment has since become an enduring symbol of one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history."
"Now we find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script," he said.

Mr. Trump on Wednesday said there was an "indication" Iran was looking to develop chemical or biological weapons because the U.S. had "shut them out" of obtaining nuclear weapons, though he offered no evidence to support the claim.
Iran war powers measure again falls short in Senate

The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.

In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.

Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.
The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic.
Trump says he's "not rushing" to make decision on Iran, will wait until new year
President Trump told Channel 12 News in Israel that he is in no hurry to make any decisions on the war with Iran, and could in fact wait until next year.
"I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran," Mr. Trump told Keshet 12's Barak Ravid, who spoke to the president as he returned from China. "We'll see what happens after the new year starts."
The story noted Mr. Trump could also change his mind, though.

The tone seems in line with his and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments from last week. Mr. Trump called new strikes "quite unlikely," while Rubio said new strikes weren't needed since the economic sanctions campaign was working so well.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he had no need to ask China or Russia for help with an Iran deal.

"They want to make a deal, so I don't need help," Mr. Trump told the network. "I mean, I'm not going to go in asking for help. And frankly, they've treated us very well. They haven't fired. They haven't put ships in the water."

articles.headline: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
keyFacts: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed he proved the Riemann hypothesis, a major unsolved math problem, using the AI tool Claude.
Alpöge's proposed solution has not been independently verified, and Anthropic has not commented on his announcement.
To qualify for the Millennium Prize, a solution must withstand at least two years of global mathematics community scrutiny.
body: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.

Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”

Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”

In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.

OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.

Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.headline: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster opening
keyFacts: Anthropic's share price dropped more than 10% on Friday to about $87.30, one day after its Nasdaq debut.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering.
Analysts said trading volatility was expected because Anthropic was the first frontier AI firm to go public.
body: - Published
Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.headline: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68 billion
keyFacts: Bending Spoons acquired email marketing firm Mailchimp from Intuit for $3.68 billion in a cash and stock deal.
Intuit originally acquired Mailchimp for roughly $12 billion in 2021, taking a loss on the sale.
Intuit told Reuters the sale will let it focus on AI tools for small businesses and repurchase shares.
body: Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

Worse yet, the cops have never been easier to set off. Some will even attack you for filming them arresting someone else.
